message.content: {"summary": "Richard Stallman, founder of the Free Software Movement, argues that the current software and copyright system is fundamentally flawed because it restricts user freedom. He traces the problem to the early 1980s, when proprietary software was copyrighted and binary-only, preventing users from studying, modifying, or sharing programs, which he views as a form of oppression. Stallman contends that Digital Rights Management (DRM) is an evil technology designed to enforce this restriction by making software secret or technically unchangeable, comparing it to shackles that cannot be removed. He criticizes modern applications of this model, including DRM in cars and tractors (citing John Deere), and the W3C's Encrypted Media Extensions (EME) which force browsers to support DRM, threatening the existence of free browsers. Regarding legal reform, Stallman proposes that all practical software (like textbooks) should be free, but he opposes making the distribution of non-free software a crime, arguing criminalization fails. He also rejects the term 'piracy,' defining it as 'sharing,' and refuses to use terms like 'protected' which imply restriction. He is skeptical of the Free Software Foundation's ability to influence government legislation and expresses strong distrust of modern packaging formats like Snap and Flatpak, viewing them as mechanisms that hide non-free software and prevent community maintenance and control."}
